items.scenario: An ops manager uploads a 4,800-row ticket export and immediately asks 'Is P1 resolution getting worse?' Claude replies that P1 is 'roughly 40% worse this quarter'.
items.question: What is the best next step?
options: Ask for data profiling first, then quarterly figures computed with code, code shown
Accept the figure, since the trend direction matches what the whole team has felt
Ask Claude how confident it is in the 40% figure, and keep it if Claude answers 'high'
Ask for a chart of the 40% change so the point lands clearly in the ops review
items.explanation: 'Roughly' signals a prose estimate. Profile first, so that duplicates, open tickets and bad timestamps are known. Then compute with code so the figure can be recomputed.
distractors: Matching a hunch isn't verification; an estimate can confirm a wrong belief.
A model's stated confidence carries no information about whether the number is correct.
Charting an unverified estimate just makes the wrong number more persuasive.

items.scenario: Claude computed utilisation per engineer with pandas and printed a table. The delivery lead will use the team average in a staffing decision tomorrow.
items.question: How should you verify the key figure?
options: Ask Claude in the same chat to double-check its calculation step by step
Rerun the same code in the same chat and compare the two outputs line by line
Read the code for filters, units and drops, then recompute independently in a sheet
Accept it as final, since any figure produced by executed code is always going to be right
items.explanation: Code makes a figure recomputable, not automatically correct. Read the code for wrong filters, units or silent drops. Then recompute the decision figure in a different tool, so a shared wrong assumption can't hide.
distractors: A same-chat self-check shares the same assumptions and can repeat the error.
Rerunning identical code reproduces the identical mistake.
Executed code can compute the wrong thing perfectly: a wrong filter or unit still runs.

items.scenario: A generated analysis of cloud costs merged a billing export with a service-owner table. Every total looks about 30% higher than finance's figures.
items.question: Which code issue should you suspect first?
options: The model rounded figures to two decimal places in the output
A join that duplicated rows, inflating every sum computed after it
The chart used a logarithmic axis that distorted how the totals compared
The CSV was too large for Claude to read in full
items.explanation: A merge where the lookup table has repeated keys duplicates rows, and every sum after it inflates. Joins are one of the five things to check in generated code.
distractors: Rounding to two decimals can't produce a 30% gap.
An axis scale changes the picture, not the computed totals.
Executed code reads every row; file size wouldn't inflate totals.

items.scenario: For a quarterly review, Claude produced a bar chart of P1 resolution time by quarter. The y-axis starts at 2.5 hours, so Q3's bar looks twice as tall as Q2's even though the values differ by 15%.
items.question: What should you change before the chart goes into the deck?
options: Keep it, because the axis labels are technically accurate
Switch to a 3D bar chart to make the values easier to compare
Add a note to the speaker script explaining the true size of the difference
Start the bar axis at zero, label units, and state n and any exclusions
items.explanation: A truncated bar axis exaggerates the difference and misleads the decision. Bars start at zero, axes carry units, and the caption states n and exclusions.
distractors: Accurate labels don't fix a misleading visual; people read bar height, not tick labels.
3D adds distortion, not honesty.
The slide misleads anyone who reads it without the script; fix the chart itself.

items.scenario: Sales asks for a pipeline summary by stage and quarter. The CRM export includes contact names, emails, phone numbers and free-text deal notes about client strategy.
items.question: What should you do before uploading?
options: Upload the full export, since the organisation uses an approved plan
Drop contact details and notes; keep only the stage, value, date and owner needed
Upload the full export but tell Claude not to mention any names
Ask Claude to delete the personal columns itself once it has loaded and read the full file
items.explanation: The question needs aggregates. Minimise before upload so personal data and client confidences never reach a place the question didn't need them. An approved plan doesn't change minimisation.
distractors: An approved plan governs where data may go, not whether unnecessary data should go at all.
An instruction about the output doesn't stop the data being uploaded and processed.
Deletion after upload is too late; the data has already been shared.

items.scenario: Before asking any business questions about a 5,000-row timesheet export, you want to know what you're dealing with.
items.question: Which first prompt best fits Practitioner practice?
options: 'Look through this whole data set and tell me the most interesting insights and trends you find.'
'Summarise this file in three bullets for my manager, with the headline numbers first.'
'Using code, profile types, missing values, duplicates, outliers. List issues; no conclusions.'
'Clean the data however you think is best, then give me the totals for each region.'
items.explanation: Profiling first, as its own step, surfaces the data issues that would otherwise silently shape every answer, and leaves the cleaning decisions with you.
distractors: An open-ended insight request skips profiling and invites plausible, unverifiable patterns.
Summarising for a manager comes after you know the data is sound.
Unlogged cleaning hands your decisions to the model and hides what was changed.

items.scenario: Claude generated an XLSX budget for the finance partner, who will adjust assumptions and re-check the totals in Excel next week.
items.question: What should you ask Claude to make sure of in the workbook?
options: Totals are live formulas referencing the input cells, not pasted values
All numbers are pasted in as values so that they can't change by accident
Each sheet contains a chart so the workbook is easy to read
The workbook is saved as a PDF copy to prevent edits
items.explanation: The reader will change assumptions and recompute. Live formulas let them trace and recompute every figure, while pasted values break that.
distractors: Pasted values freeze the numbers, so changed assumptions silently don't flow through.
Charts don't help someone tracing how a total is computed.
A PDF blocks the very editing the finance partner needs to do.

items.scenario: Your variance report says cloud spend was over plan 'mainly due to higher usage'. The finance partner asks what's missing.
items.question: Which revision best meets the reporting standard?
options: Add a sentence saying the analysis was done carefully, with AI assistance, and reviewed
Give the variance size, its sized drivers, and the caveats and assumptions
Replace the sentence with a chart of monthly spend and no text
Lengthen the narrative with more detail on each cloud service used
items.explanation: A variance narrative gives actual against plan with absolute and % deltas, then names the drivers with their sizes and states the assumptions and caveats, each traceable to computed figures.
distractors: Saying the analysis was done carefully adds nothing a reader can check.
A chart without stated drivers and caveats leaves the explanation to guesswork.
More detail without sizes and caveats is more words, not a better explanation.

items.scenario: Claude's code-based analysis prints a P1 mean of 9.8 hours, but its written summary says 'P1 tickets average about 8 hours'. The code and output look correct.
items.question: What does this tell you about where to check?
options: Nothing important, because the difference is within normal rounding
The code must be wrong, so rerun the analysis from scratch
The executed figure should be trusted over the code, so remove the code from the report
Prose can drift from computed output; check the narrative against the printed results
items.explanation: Executed code makes the printed figure reproducible, but Claude writes the summary afterwards and can misquote it. Every number in the narrative must match the printed output.
distractors: 9.8 versus 'about 8' is not rounding; it's a misquote.
The executed output is consistent; the drift is in the prose written afterwards.
Removing the code removes recomputability, which is the point of the module.

items.scenario: A P1 mean resolution time jumped from 3.1 to 4.4 hours between quarters, while the median stayed at 2.0 hours. There were 48 P1 tickets in the latest quarter.
items.question: What is the most defensible reading before claiming P1 handling got worse?
options: Handling clearly got worse, because the mean rose by over 40%
Handling clearly improved, because the median is now well below the mean
A few outliers likely moved the mean, so inspect them before claiming a trend
The data is unusable, because a mean and a median should always match closely
items.explanation: Durations are right-skewed. A stable median with a rising mean on a small n usually means a few long tickets. Look at the outliers and report both statistics before you claim a trend.
distractors: A mean-only reading on skewed data with n=48 can be one ticket.
Median below mean is normal for skewed data; it says nothing about improvement.
Means and medians differ for all skewed data; that's expected, not a defect.
